desc:
A long bench has n seats numbered 0 to n - 1. Students arrive one at a time and nobody ever leaves.

The first student sits at seat 0. Every later student picks the free seat whose distance to the closest seated student is as large as possible; if several seats give the same largest distance, the one with the smallest number is taken.

Return the seat taken by the k-th student (counting from 1).

n = 10: the seats are taken in the order 0, 9, 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8
n = 10, k = 4  -> 2
n = 10, k = 10 -> 8
hints: Simulating over all n seats per student is far too slow. Think about the free stretches between seated students instead.
Each stretch between two seated students has one best seat (its middle, the smaller one on ties) and a known distance. The stretch behind the last seated student also needs a rule.

Keep the best seat of every stretch in a heap ordered by (largest distance, smallest seat). Pop the best, then split its stretch into two new stretches. The end of the bench (seat n-1) starts as a one-sided stretch with distance n-1.
editorial: After the first student sits at seat 0, the free seats form stretches. A stretch strictly between seated students at l < r offers its best seat at (l + r) // 2 with distance (r - l) // 2. The only one-sided stretch is the tail after the last seated student; its best seat is n - 1 at distance n - 1 - l, because there is no second neighbour. (No head stretch exists since seat 0 is taken first.)

The global choice at each step is the best candidate over all stretches, which is the minimum of the tuples (-distance, seat) in a heap. Taking a seat splits its stretch into two interior stretches whose candidates are pushed. Only k pops are needed, so the work is O(k log k) no matter how large n is.
